title: Starter integration runway: mental models and checklist
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a compact, opinionated companion for the first-run developer experience when integrating Redwood SDKs into an application. It focuses on the high-level mental models we want users to internalize, an actionable first-15-minute checklist, minimal sample commands for JS/Python, and quick notes on telemetry + fallbacks.

Audience:
- Software engineers shipping their first Redwood call in an hour
- SDK authors and docs writers who need an aligned checklist for copy
- Solutions engineers running onboarding sessions

Design goals (why this file exists):
- Reduce cognitive load: present 3 mental models instead of a feature dump
- Make a friction-free first success path (15m) with concrete commands
- Surface the most common failure modes and immediate mitigations
- Provide lightweight telemetry guidance so teams ship observability by default

Core mental models (short):
1) One API surface, many deployment modes — same call, different guarantees:
   - Concept: treat "redwood client" like a networked LLM service. Code doesn't change whether the backend is Hosted, Dedicated, or Private.
   - Practical: configs are runtime knobs (region, model_alias, routing_policy). Examples in quickstart use these keys.

2) Latency vs batch cost tradeoff is explicit and visible:
   - Concept: per-request latency is separate from per-token cost. Batching/caching reduces cost but can increase median latency.
   - Practical: show how to set batch_tolerance and prefix_cache in examples.

3) Failure is graceful if you wire fallbacks:
   - Concept: optimistic path (fast low-cost model) + fallback path (higher-SLO model) is the recommended pattern.
   - Practical: include a small SDK helper that swaps model on 5xx/timeouts.

15-minute checklist (first-success path):
- [ ] Create account + API key (Hosted) or retrieve endpoint + cert (Private)
- [ ] Install SDK (npm / pip) and verify version >= minimal supported
- [ ] Set env var REDWOOD_API_KEY or REDWOOD_ENDPOINT + REDWOOD_AUTH_CERT_PATH
- [ ] Run the "hello world" sample below and confirm streaming/complete response
- [ ] Confirm metadata appears in Console (route, model, latency) within 1 min
- [ ] Enable sample telemetry labels: service=my-service;env=dev
- [ ] Add a simple retry-on-5xx wrapper (see snippet)

Minimal quickstart snippets (copy/paste):
JS (Node) minimal:
const { Redwood } = require('@redwood-inference/sdk');
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, model: 'redwood-mini-v1' });
(async () => {
  const res = await client.generate({ prompt: 'Summarize: Redwood inference platform', max_tokens: 120 });
  console.log(res.text);
})();

Python minimal:
from redwood import Redwood
client = Redwood(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'], model='redwood-mini-v1')
print(client.generate(prompt='Summarize: Redwood inference platform', max_tokens=120).text)

Quick config examples (runtime knobs):
- model: 'redwood-mini-v1' | 'redwood-std-v1'
- routing_policy: 'latency' | 'cost' | 'region'
- batch_tolerance_ms: 5 | 25 | 50
- prefix_cache: true | false

Telemetry & observability (must-haves for first deploy):
- Emit: route_id, model_id, client_version, aws_region/zone (if Dedicated/Private)
- Capture: request_id, latency_ms, error_type (timeout, 5xx, model_error), cost_units_token
- Console sanity: confirm a single sample request shows in Console within ~1 minute; otherwise check telemetry ingestion key
- Suggested sampling: full traces for first 100 requests, then 1% when stable

Failure modes & quick mitigations:
- Auth errors: check API key vs endpoint, watch 401s in logs — common cause: wrong env var name or expired key
- Network timeouts: set a client-level timeout shorter than HTTP proxy default and add retry (exponential backoff, jitter)
- Cold model spin-up: route to lower-latency variant for interactive flows; configure warm_pools for Dedicated customers
- High token cost: enable prefix_cache and reduce max_tokens or switch to cheaper model for pre-processing tasks

Rollout plan (micro):
- Canary: route 5% traffic to new model or SDK version for 24h; monitor latency queries and error rate
- Metric thresholds: +20% latency or +0.5% absolute error rate -> rollback or increase canary window

Developer-facing helper snippets (pseudo):
retryGenerate(prompt) {
  try { return await client.generate(prompt); } catch (e) {
    if (isTransient(e)) { await sleep(backoff()); return await client.generate(prompt, { model: 'redwood-std-v1' }); }
    throw e;
  }
}

Docs notes for writers (what to include in the long-form doc):
- Small decision tree: interactive vs batch vs embedder (pick models and knobs)
- Table comparing common settings and expected perf/cost outcomes
- FAQ: "Which model for cheap REPL?" "How to test private endpoints locally?"
- Troubleshooting appendix with the most common Console traces and what they mean

Unresolved questions / open items:
- Should the SDK set a default sampling policy for telemetry labels or leave it to the app? (tradeoff: ease vs PII risk)
- Do we provide a built-in fallback decorator or ship examples only? (SE time to implement vs API surface)
- Rate-limiting UX: should per-key limits return a specific error type that SDK maps to a RetryableError?

Next steps (owner: Marina):
1) Convert this to a 1-page quickstart in the docs site (deadline: 2026-02-28)
2) Add a small code example repository with the exact above snippets for JS/Python (owner: Tom)
3) Propose an SDK helper for fallbacks and get SE feedback (owner: Raj)

Notes to self / meeting followups:
- Pair with Console infra to ensure first-request trace appears within 60s for Hosted flows
- Run a 15-minute test with Solutions Eng workshop and capture friction points

End of doc.
